utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And General Talic, I put the same question to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I can hear and I can understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, my name is Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor. Ms. Korner will not be with us today, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman here with Tania Radosavljevic, Milka Maglov, and Milos Peric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, replacing Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron. And I'm assisted by Mr. Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, at this distance you feel safer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Somewhat, Your Honour. It's a little harder for you to pull my leg from that far away, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start. Please call in Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to be kindly requested to make the same solemn declaration that you made twice already yesterday, and we can proceed after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Cayley will be continuing, proceeding with his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if you could remember to pause between my question and your answer, because as you know, we're speaking the same language, and there is interpretation between us into two other languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We may not be quite speaking the same language. I shall endeavour to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can just recap briefly on what you were discussing yesterday. You referred to the change of name of the ZOBK to the ARK on the 16th of September of 1991. And if I can now refer you to Tab 14, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 17. What document is this, first of all, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the shorthand notes of the second session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Just because I know we will return to the first session shortly, the first session of this assembly was convened and constituted on the 24th of October, 1991, and so this is the next, second session, on 21 November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, could you please repeat the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Behind tab 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, specifically concentrating on these autonomous regions that were being created at the time, if you go to page 29, and explain to the Judges the significance of what is said there in these minutes, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This page reflects the decision of the second Assembly of the Serbian People to verify the existence of five autonomous regions. These regions were constituted in ways that were somewhat similar to the constitution of -- the creation of the ZOBK and then, in this particular document, ratified or verified by the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is the Autonomous Region of Krajina specifically referred to in this verification by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is the first one referenced in the second line of the decision, along with its - I believe it's 20 at that point - members who -- municipalities whose assemblies had declared association with the Autonomous Region of Krajina, or ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the -- were the municipalities that are listed here the final constituent members of this Autonomous Region of Krajina, or did it change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It changed. It evolved over time. In fact, I believe there is an entry in the Official Gazette also reflecting this decision. It also lists 20 municipalities but they are not the same 20. There is a variance of two of them. So this question of exactly who belonged at any given time, I think, is a rather difficult one to define precisely, at least from this level, from the level of the ARK itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can now move ahead, and if I can refer you to page 55 of your report, and specifically the section which you have subtitled "Arms Buildup," now, you identify in your report various paramilitary groups that were linked with the specific political parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina and I would like you to address each one of those so that the Judges get an accurate picture of the connections between these forces and the various political parties in the country at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each of the three national parties, the SDA, SDS and HDZ, formed or operated paramilitaries, starting in no later than the summer of 1991. For the SDA, those paramilitaries really had two principal names, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. Both the HDZ and SDS also became involved with paramilitaries from neighbouring states, that is Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro. The Serbian paramilitaries were known by a variety of names. They were organised by, among others, the leader of the Serbian Renewal Movement, Vuk Draskovic, the Serbian -- Bosnian-born Serb, Vojislav Seselj, and Zeljko Raznatovic. In addition, there was at least one Serbian military, paramilitary, operating from the Serbian Krajina region of Croatia. The difference of -- that kind of came to be the important factor in these paramilitaries was really the existing organisation of defence of Yugoslavia, and that consisted really of two parts: Number 1, the JNA, the Yugoslav National Army; and second, the Territorial Defence, known as the TO. The military planning in socialist Yugoslavia never really departed from the Partisan experience in World War II, and part of this thinking was that at any given time, small sectors of the country should be able to conduct resistance based on local forces. These were the Territorial Defence forces, which had their own weapons - they were light weapons - and in the late socialist period, developed a dual reporting relationship to the JNA and to the republican authorities in which they were located. In September 1990, the JNA issued an order to bring the arms of the Territorial Defence forces under control of the JNA, essentially put them under lock and key in JNA armouries. This did something but not a great deal to limit the arms capabilities of these TO units, which in the course of 1991 came -- and in early 1992, came under the control of the political leadership in whatever municipality they were located. So for example, the TO units in the area under the control of the Bosnian central government became either part of the -- typically became a part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and in Croat-controlled areas became a part of the Croatian Defence Council, HVO; and in Serb-controlled areas came under the control of the SDS or later on the JNA, and ultimately the Army of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if I can just interrupt you briefly, because you referred to a document that we won't go through. But you referred to the document where the JNA essentially placed under their control the arms of the Territorial Defence, and I think that document is at Tab 16, Prosecutor's Exhibit 19. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Prosecutor's 19, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final tie-breaker in this picture, really, was the JNA, which in the summer of 1991 engaged certain commanders, certain units -- engaged in distribution of light arms to SDS committees and Serbian paramilitary groups in Bosnia. The JNA subsequently underwent a transformation over many months, a transformation which really was not complete until the summer of 1992 but involved the increasing, if one might call it, Bosnianisation of the JNA in Bosnia. First of all, the JNA was -- the JNA's presence in Bosnia was strengthened by the withdrawal of JNA forces from Croatia in the late month or two of 1991 and early 1992. Then, more significantly, the JNA in Bosnia underwent some transformation of its personnel. This process is reported by Borislav Jovic, the close advisor to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and also a member of the Presidency -- of the Federal Presidency of Yugoslavia, in which he described a meeting on the 5th of December to transfer all non-Bosnian soldiers out of Bosnia and transfer all Bosnians who were stationed in JNA units elsewhere back into Bosnia. And later in December, he reported that that process of stationing Bosnian troops -- troops native to Bosnia in Bosnia was largely complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just a few points of clarification. And if I can refer you to your report. You've essentially identified three types of armed formations in Bosnia during this time period: paramilitary formations, Territorial Defence, and the JNA. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I have just been -- had my attention drawn that I should call on you to move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll move the microphone closer to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I think that's clear enough on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In terms of heavy weapons in Bosnia, armour, artillery, who had in their possession these heavy weapons during this time period and subsequently into 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA had a virtually complete monopoly on heavy weapons. And by "heavy weapons," I mean heavy artillery, aircraft, tanks, and armoured personnel carriers, things like this, that -- right up until, really, the spring of 1992. Those were in the sole possession of the JNA with perhaps a very occasional exception. But none of the efforts to arm locals involved heavy weapons at that point, until that time, say, early spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you state in your report that on the 15th of April of 1992, TO units in Muslim-led municipalities were placed under a unified command and became the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, we are calling other military experts but, to your knowledge, in April of 1992, how effective was that unified command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't answer the question for a specific area, but I think in general, the effectiveness was best closest to -- in and closest to Sarajevo, and became less effective and less direct in those areas that were removed from Sarajevo and in which local TO units were often very poorly armed and had problems communicating with the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just referring briefly to the region of the Krajina, from your knowledge, if you can answer this question, how effective was the Bosnian army in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I don't really think there was a Bosnian army per se in the Krajina. It was really these local TO units which were poorly armed and its effectiveness was very low.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you do state that the Bosnian army had the advantage in terms of manpower; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appears that at this time, yes, they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can move on to page 58 of your report, and this is the section that is titled, "Towards independence and division of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now we are moving back to events at the republican level, and if you could tell the Court briefly about the various solutions that were sought to the Yugoslav problem in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first half of 1991, the presidents of the six republics of Yugoslavia held a rotating series of talks. One president hosted each talk in his respective capital. These began in January and ended in June, and featured kind of an alignment of the Slovenian and Croatian leaderships promoting a loose confederation, and the Serbian and Montenegrin leaderships supporting a strong federal Yugoslavia, with efforts for compromise being brokered principally by Presidents Izetbegovic and Tupurkovski of Bosnia and Montenegro respectively. In the course of these meetings, there was another meeting at Karadjordjevo at the royal hunting estate in Serbia, between Presidents Tudjman of Croatia and Milosevic of Serbia. In this discussion, which they held among just the two of them, although there were many other members of their parties nearby, they held a conversation about a possible division of Bosnia. They did not, by all accounts, agree at this time on such a partition. Rather, they established a commission to investigate the possibility of an agreement, and this commission held a couple of sessions and adjourned without reaching an agreement. This would be the first of a number of efforts between Serbs -- Serb and Croat leaders to reach an agreement on the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After the last meeting of the six republican presidents -- at the last meeting, there was an agreement to pursue further talks between Presidents Tudjman, Milosevic and Izetbegovic. That meeting took place shortly thereafter in Split and, again, by -- a number of accounts suggest that partition was openly discussed at that meeting among the -- those three presidents. I think after the conclusion of these talks, which failed essentially to reach an agreement on the future of a federal Yugoslavia, they were followed very soon by the war in Slovenia. And at that point, discussions among the Yugoslav republics essentially became internationalised, first through the intervention of the troika of the European Community and later the semi-permanent, ultimately permanent Conference on the Former Yugoslavia under UN and EC auspices.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, let's go back to Bosnia, to October of 1991, and to the republican assembly in Sarajevo. 15th of October, 1991, Radovan Karadzic is speaking before the assembly. What does he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a session of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina on October 15, Dr. Karadzic delivered an impassioned speech in which he raised the prospect that if the Muslims pursued the option of independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they might cease to exist. In response to that comment or that very impassioned presentation, President Izetbegovic and -- President of the SDA and of Bosnia-Herzegovina, responded that the manner of Karadzic's presentation and the message that he conveyed aptly illustrated why Bosnia and Herzegovina might no longer be able to remain a part of the Yugoslav federation. On that same day, after the assembly had adjourned for the day, and been adjourned by its president, SDS President or member Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serbia -- or the Croatian and Muslim representatives of the HDZ and SDA remained and reconvened on their authority the assembly, and passed a declaration of sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was exactly the step that was bitterly opposed by the SDS, and at least in symbolic terms, moved Bosnia and Herzegovina one step closer to independence. On that evening, there was a session of the SDS board, and I -- this meeting appears to me to be a definitive discussion of strategy and launch a new course for the SDS for the next several months. In that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if I can just interrupt you, this meeting that you refer to, that happened on the evening of the 15th of October of 1991, the meeting of the SDS board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the minutes of that meeting are at Tab 17, Prosecutor's Exhibit 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could go through those minutes and identify for the Court those sections that you believe are important in respect of events that were accelerating at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 2 of this document in the English version, Professor Milorad Ekmecic is speaking. And in the very end of the first full paragraph on that page he says: "The Serbs have created regions which are not connected, and these regions must not be allowed to establish their governments which would not be connected. In public, we must let it be known that we can set up a Serbian government with its seat in Sarajevo which would connect all our regions." So Professor Ekmecic, who was a Professor of History in Sarajevo and kind of a key senior elder member of the SDS, here expressly advocates the formation of a republic-level Serbian government. He is followed by Mr. Dutina, who says: "This evening we must get rid of the illusion that a form of life together with the Muslims and Croats can be found." Going to the fourth page, just turning the page, the -- Mr. Radovan Neskovic says in a number of comments making recommendations, number one: "Since they will not revoke their decisions, I suggest that a parliamentary crisis be provoked." Now, this comment is -- relates to the disagreement among party leaders about whether SDS members should continue to participate in the deliberative bodies and institutions of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It -- all parties operated on the assumption that if a large number of delegates withdrew from a deliberative body, this in some sense invalidated or weakened the authority of that body and was therefore referred to here as a parliamentary crisis. He adds then: "We should demand new elections, because in this way we would gain time, which suits us." Point four is "Go for a change of policy with the aim of creating a greater Serbia." Now, this pertains to that dispute that arose at the time of the creation of our declaration of unity of two Krajinas. The party's policy, the SDS official policy at this time, was to support a federal Yugoslavia and only to view the creation of a greater Serbia as a back-up or contingent strategy. So Neskovic here is proposing that the party now move to that back-up or reserve strategy and support the creation of a greater Serbia. It will be seen that that viewpoint does not prevail within the party at this time. Going to the next speaker, Rajko Dukic, who was a very important member of the SDS, President of its cadre commission. Point 2: "We cannot leave the assembly or any other body." Dukic and many others believed that the SDS should continue to work within the deliberative bodies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's in the comments of Mr. Miskin halfway down this page that we find many of the recommendations that were in fact implemented in the subsequent 1993 months. Number one: "Continue regionalisation more intensively." And "regionalisation," as I'll show shortly, had a rather complex meaning at this time. Number four: "Establish parallel government bodies immediately so that they will be ready." Number five: "Organise militarily, especially in the towns, and give instructions to this effect in the municipal boards and local boards." And number six: "We are not well organised in the media war." And then number seven, he mentions a plebiscite. To the next speaker, Mr. Tutnjevic. On the following page, which is the next to last page containing English language text: "We must call on the JNA to secure the bridges on the Drina." This was intended to secure free passage of goods and materiel from Serbia to Bosnia. "The regions must be ready to impose a blockade of commodity and money channels towards Sarajevo." And finally: "Urgently issue a proclamation setting out the political goals of the Serbian people." Professor Slavko Leovac, who was another senior academic and influential member of the SDS, noted in point two of his presentation that "a republic in which there are three ethnic groups, two of which are linked to their mother countries, cannot be neutral." And finally the last sentence in the document, Biljana Plavsic, a member of the Presidency, states that "the demilitarisation of the JNA is out of the question because a concentration of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina has already been announced." This comment pertains to the concentration of forces in Bosnia in the wake of the conflict in Slovenia -- or in Croatia and in support of the military effort there. Now, the primary -- this meeting came to no formally established recommendations, but the primary events that occurred in the next three months were already recommended or backed by one of these speakers. Those were: First of all, the formation of a Serbian assembly, which took place on the 24th of October, 1991; second, the holding of a plebiscite of the Serbian people; and third, the formation of a Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was completed on 9 January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you've already referred to the Serbian assembly meeting of the 24th of October of 1991, and if we can briefly look at the minutes of that constituting session, which are behind tab 18, Prosecutor's Exhibit 21, and if you could first of all go to page 36 of those minutes, and that page contains the address on the establishment of a Serbian assembly, and if you could draw the Judges' attention to those significant areas of Mr. Najdanovic's speech on the matter of the establishment of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These words were spoken at the time that the decision to constitute this assembly was under consideration, and there are two indications that the speaker is Mr. Milutin Najdanovic. There is a change of tapes here right in the middle of his presentation, before his name is mentioned the second time. The first comment I would -- or comment of his that I would note is that just before his name is mentioned the second time, he states, "The Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be comprised of the deputies of the SDS and of the Serbian Renewal Movement in the Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly." So this new body consists of deputies in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina of Serbian nationality from two particular parties. The second paragraph after the change of tape, "The Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall debate and decide on issues pertaining to the achievement of equality by the Serbian people with other peoples and nationalities living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to protection of the interests of the Serbian people should such interests be put at risk by any decisions reached by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly." His next sentence pertains to this SDS decision to remain in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. organs, the deliberative bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "The Serbian deputies shall continue working in the chambers and working bodies of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly to which they were elected until a final solution is found to the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia." And then one paragraph down, "The Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall recognise the validity of enactments by the Bosnia and Herzegovina assembly, provided they are not contrary to the interests of the Serbian people." I think this speech really represents the spirit and intent of the formation of this assembly as a Serbian-only body devoted to protecting Serb interests against what -- against the -- whatever decisions might be reached by the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, you also stated earlier that this same meeting decided that a plebiscite would be held of the Serbian people in Bosnia, and if I can direct you to page 41 of these minutes, which refers to that decision, and if you can explain to the Judges exactly what the purpose of that plebiscite was and who was to participate in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision to hold a plebiscite was reached at this assembly. It was to be a plebiscite of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Others were allowed to vote but they voted on a separate coloured ballot, a yellow ballot, and their votes were tabulated separately, subsequent to this referendum -- or plebiscite, on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991. The assembly, in point 2 of this decision on page 41, essentially states that the decision to remain within Yugoslavia will enter into a -- into force on the day it is confirmed at this plebiscite of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the question at the plebiscite raised asked each voter to choose whether they wished to remain as part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to the results of the plebiscite, and they are contained in the session of the assembly that was held on the 21st of November of 1991, and unfortunately that involves moving backwards in the file to tab 14, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 15 of that document, which is Prosecutor's 17, in the English language variant, the commission for the plebiscite reported the results, and it indicates here that there were over a million votes in favour of the issue on the plebiscite and 398 votes against. On the following page, page 16, there is also an indication that Serbs were allowed to vote in foreign countries. So the last paragraph on that page reports, "The speaker is pleased to inform us that 916 people voted in Sweden, all in favour; 353 voted in the U.S.; some in Great Britain, Germany, Switzerland, and some 30.000 people in Soviet Russia, all of whom voted in favour."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Muslim and Croat people of Bosnia-Herzegovina participate in this plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of Muslims and Croats did not participate in the plebiscite, did not vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in essence, this was a vote of the Serbian people rather than anybody else in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What in essence was the result of the plebiscite, in terms of what did the people, the Serbian people of Bosnia decide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian people or Serbs of Bosnia voted overwhelmingly to remain in Yugoslavia. In addition, in at least two municipalities, another vote was taken at the same time. In the municipality of Bosanska Krupa and in Donji Vakuf, Serbs were asked another question, given another box, presumably, on the ballot, to ask if they wished to remain a part of Yugoslavia but also a part of a Serbian Assembly of that municipality. So, for example, on page 31 of this same document, the speaker is Mr. Miroslav Vjestica, representative of Bosanska Krupa, and at the very top of the page, he says, "We held a referendum of the Serbian people of Bosanska Krupa municipality along with the plebiscite of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and formed our own municipality called the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa, since 63 per cent of the present territory of Bosanska Krupa municipality belongs to the Serbian people. In this way, the Serbian people of Bosanska Krupa municipality made the decision to stay a part of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka and through it a part of Yugoslavia." And on the very top of page 34, we have the representative from Donji Vakuf, who is not identified, say, "Mr. President, people's deputies, ladies and gentlemen, as regards item one of the decision, I would like to ask that we add the people of Donji Vakuf, who added another box on 9 and 10 November on the plebiscite and decided to live in the ARK then. We would like to ask that Donji Vakuf be added to the list on behalf of the 7500 Serbs in Donji Vakuf municipality." Then immediately after that, Mr. Djukic from Olovo makes a similar statement, saying they also added a second box and -- Olovo never joined the ARK, but it, subsequent to this, was listed as part of the SAO of Romanija. Consequently, this plebiscite also served as a vehicle for Serbs in non-Serb majority municipalities to, in a sense, declare they were bypassing the established assembly and affiliate themselves with the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've specifically stated that these municipalities did not have a Serbian majority - Bosanska Krupa, Donji Vakuf - and if I can refer you briefly to your report, page 48, where you have the ethnic census and those two municipalities are contained in that second table, what was the ethnic composition of those two municipalities, Krupa and Donji Vakuf, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is page 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 49.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It will show that Bosanski Krupa was -- in 1991 was 24 per cent Serbs and 74 per cent Muslims. Donji Vakuf, its population was 39 per cent Serbs and 55 per cent Muslims and 3 per cent Croats. In each there was a -- and also a small percentage of Yugoslavs and others. So both were 24 and 39 per cent Serbian at this time in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Muslims were in the majority in both of these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can now move back to Tab 21, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 24. And this is a transcript of the third session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is page 63 of your report, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this session I think is significant for the decision to establish Serbian municipalities. And if I can direct you firstly to page 13 of this document, and if you could briefly summarise for the Judges the discussion that took place during this particular meeting of the SDS -- of the Serbian Assembly. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Much of this meeting was taken up with a discussion of the topic of regionalisation, and there was an effort to define "regionalisation" and determine what the next steps would be. One of the early speakers in this debate, Mr. Veselinovic on page 13 advocates in the second paragraph of his speech: "I think that the order of moves should be planned plainly speaking to break up the existing municipalities where Serbs are not in a majority, for there are situations of some adjacent local communities of settlements belonging to two municipalities where Serbs are not a majority. This means that from two or three neighbouring municipalities, we have space to form a large nice Serbian municipality." This is that variant of regionalisation I referred to early on in which municipalities were essentially carved up, their Serbian inhabitants identified, and then either join a new -- an existing municipality or form a new one. On the next page, page 14, the chairman, who is Momcilo Krajisnik, states in the last paragraph of his presentation that "only municipalities where Serb delegates are a minority should form such assemblies, as this republican assembly of ours, so as to exercise certain rights. I think that this is the source of the misunderstanding. Veselinovic spoke about regionalisation, the rounding off of territories, like Mr. Vjestica and others are doing." And Mr. Vjestica, of course, was the representative of Bosanska Krupa who had reported on the formation of a Serbian municipality that then affiliated itself with the ARK. But at this point, as evidenced by this paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik supported the formation of these Serbian assemblies only in those municipalities where Serbs were in a minority. On page 22, at the top of the page -- the speaker here is Mr. Rajko Dukic. He's identified on the previous page, page 21, only as Rajko, but I believe that he is -- it's quite clearly Mr. Dukic, based on his other views expressed on regionalisation. "I therefore propose that serious work be done on the issue of regionalisation, not only as a political issue but also as a strategic one where we also have a specific goal. It is necessary to define not only the territorial relationships but also economic, culture, and all other ones." And then if I could turn to page 28, after this discussion which included varying views on exactly what ought to be included in the regionalisation process, at the bottom of the page, the chairman asks for an adoption of a resolution and also mentions a couple of supplements and says that, "the assembly unanimously, with the two mentioned supplements, adopted the proposed recommendation on the establishment of municipal assemblies of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And the chairman so noted, adding that the cover letter would specify that "this is recommended where necessary and should in no case be across the board, because the latter would be unnecessary." Now, this suggests to me that as of the 11th of December, 1991, the formation of Serbian assemblies was voluntary for all SDS local boards. The reason, of course, was the extensive discussion that had gone into this decision. But as of the 11th of December, both as it is reflected here in this assembly session and in the version that subsequently appeared in the Official Gazette, this is a decision that's voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if we can now move ahead in time to the 19th of December of 1991, to an important document. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 25, and it's behind Tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like at this stage to interpose a sort of general objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether a document is important or not, and I object to Mr. Cayley identifying documents as important and crucial and -- we're getting his opinion, basically, which we shouldn't be getting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your objection is sustained, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Cayley, I think you take the point, and I'm sure you understand. So move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think somewhere in his report he makes reference to it being a critical document, but I won't state that if Mr. Ackerman has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, that particular document, the title is clear. I won't rehearse it on to the transcript. But rather than me pointing out to you areas in the document which are critical, could you go through it, essentially identify for the Judges the sections which you believe are the essence of the document and state why they are and what they actually mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With this document of 19 December, eight days after the Serbian Assembly meeting, the formation of separate Serbian institutions moved from being voluntary to being mandatory for SDS local boards. I would add that this is a somewhat complex document in my view, and it's, I think, best understood by comparing the two variants, Variants A and B. Variant A describes those municipalities in which Serbs constituted a majority of the population. That is spelled out in point three of the second -- it's the opposite side of the cover page in the English translation under -- under point capital "One," there's a "3" there in which it spells out these two variants. In addition, the document describes actions to be taken under the first stage and the second stage. So in a sense, this is a document that prescribes transition from regionalisation to a preparedness for war. And I'll just read a few excerpts from this. On the -- at page 3 of the document in the English translation, point three: "The SDS municipal board will immediately form a crisis staff of the Serbian people in the municipality." It then spells out those people who are to be members of the crisis staff in Variant A. If I can just flash to page 6, in Variant B -- on page 6, Variant B, point three, the very same directive is given: "The SDS municipal board will immediately form a crisis staff of the Serbian people." It's less detailed in spelling out who is to -- who are to be members of the crisis staff. The reason for that is that in the Variant A municipalities which were already under SDS leadership, it could be safely assumed that all those offices mentioned in Variant A were already filled by SDS appointees or those who met SDS satisfaction. Now, in Variant A, again on page 3, point four was: "To convene and proclaim an assembly of Serbian people in the municipality comprised of deputies from the ranks of Serbian people in the municipal assembly." So this echoes exactly what the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina had done on the 24th of October, take those deputies from the municipal assembly who are from the ranks of the Serbian people and proclaim a separate body. The very same recommendation is found on page 6 for Variant B, also in point four. The first stage in both variants was to create these institutions but to take only very limited steps of implementation. It remained for the second stage to actually take power in these municipalities, and the prescription for taking power was slightly different in the Variant A and Variant B cases. But if I could turn to the last page, page 8, under heading 3, the last two points, 3 and 4, specify how this process is to be triggered. Number 3, "The order to carry out the specified tasks, measures and other activities in these instructions is given exclusively by the Bosnia-Herzegovina SDS president using a secret, pre-established procedure." And then point 4, "The secret procedure for transmitting and accepting the order to carry out these tasks, measures and other activities specified in these instructions shall be established at a future time." The Variant B second stage was characterised by procedures that were more secret and which were to take place in those parts of the municipality in which a majority of Serbs lived. So, for example, on page 7, point 4, in this second implementation stage, "Those municipalities which did not have a Serbian majority were to organise the constant protection of all vital facilities, communication lines and production capabilities in inhabited areas with a majority Serbian population." And over the page now, on page 8, point 5, "In inhabited areas with a majority Serbian population, increase reserve stocks of food and other essential household products in an organised way and in other appropriate ways." I guess that means disorganised way. Number 6, "At approaches to areas inhabited by a Serbian population, organise secret patrols and an information system focusing on all possible dangers for the Serbian population." This document was very explicit about many of the steps to be undertaken, and yet it gave no deadline. There were no deadlines contained in the document, no time frame for these things to be done. However, there is a substantial record of changes throughout municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina that corresponded to the instructions contained in this document for the first stage, and in many municipalities, Serb assemblies were convened and proclaimed within days of this document being issued. There was, however, substantial resistance to it as well from some local SDS boards, and consequently, by the end of March, there were still many municipalities in which this first stage had not been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if I can just draw your attention to a number of sections. In particular, let's look at Variant B, where the Serbian population was in a minority and specifically page 7, paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- of the second stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This states that the local boards are directed to mobilise all police forces from the ranks of the Serbian people, and in cooperation with command posts and headquarters of the JNA, ensure their gradual subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, paragraph 3, to summarise it, is stating that the JNA reserve units and TO units should be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, ensure that the order is put into effect to mobilise JNA reserve forces and TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did the real authority for that order lie in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the authority to mobilise JNA reserve units was in fact a matter of great dispute, but the primary claimant was the JNA. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at a number of points, disputed that, but the mobilisation of TO units was a function of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you were to sum up this document in a very brief statement, what is this document as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a set of quite specific and detailed instructions to prepare for war, to create new institutions, to make preparations for armed conflict, and then to implement certain steps on the instructions of the SDS central leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can now move to Prosecutor's Exhibit 27, which is behind tab 24, what is this declaration? And if you can link it to the Variant A, Variant B document that we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have three pieces of paper here, which are part of P27, and the second sheet that I have is a two-sided English-language sheet, which is -- reflects a decision, if I'm correct in this, that everyone has this -- this particular document is the decision of the Serbian Municipality of Bihac to constitute itself, that is to organise, in a meeting held on December 21, 1991. There is then the first page, which is -- I don't have a translation, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, sorry, we are awaiting a translation of the first page, so if you deal simply with the decision, and you'll find the page after that, the original version --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- of the document is in place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first page is in fact a decision of the Bihac assembly to join the ARK, adopted on the -- I think on the 28th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the second decision or, in fact, it's the first decision because it's the 21st of December, 1991, the decision for which there is a translation, how many days after the instructions on Variant A, Variant B was this decision made by Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is two days after the instructions from the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did Bihac fall within the classification of Variant A or Variant B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Variant B municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So Serbs were in a minority in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, the next document that I want to refer to, we don't have a translation of that document into English. I don't know how you wish to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we point it out to the witness first. We'll see whether he is in a position to enlighten us on it, and then we can take a decision whether to proceed on it or not. Please keep in mind that we have roughly five to ten minutes more before we break and so adjust your preference to continue with the cross-examination -- with the examination-in-chief now or we break now and continue in half an hour's time. I mean, choose whatever suits you. I'm leaving you the option. I don't know how long you intend to question the witness on the next document, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Tantalisingly close to the end of this file, Your Honour, but I don't think I'm going to finish it in five minutes, but certainly I can deal with this document in five minutes. It's a short document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then proceed. Which document are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we are referring to tab 25, Prosecutor's Exhibit 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is this document, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Prijedor at its session on the 17th of January, 1992, to join the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you wish -- Mr. President, do you wish there to be a translation of this document into English? The witness can actually read it into the transcript and then the interpreters who have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very short document, Mr. Cayley. If Dr. Donia is in a position to tell us what it says, it would be easy and it will lighten our burden in any case, if he's in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can read it - it's very brief - and ask the oral translation to come through, if you wish. [Interpretation] "On the basis of the rules of procedure of the work of the assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor, at a session of the assembly held on the 17th of January, 1992, we hereby take the following decision on joining the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. Article 1: The Assembly of the Serbian People of Prijedor municipality hereby unanimously adopt" - the word is not clear, but it is probably "decision" - "on joining the Serbian territory of the Prijedor municipality of Bosanska Krajina." Article 2: This decision shall enter into force on the day of its adoption at the meeting of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Prijedor municipality. A signature by the President of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Prijedor municipality. The name is not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, if you wish, we can pause at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the Chamber will rise, and we will resume at ten to 10.00 -- at ten to 11.00. Sorry, ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please call the witness in, please, Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you had referred to the decision by Prijedor. In fact, you'd read out the decision in the original version. Now, this decision in fact not only declares a Serbian assembly in Prijedor but it also decides to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a decision to join the -- the ARK, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just to digress for a moment. Prijedor. From your knowledge, your expertise, what was the historical significance of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prijedor was a scene of considerable fighting in World War II, and in fact a major battle was fought in -- near Prijedor between the Partisans and the Germans with their Ustasha allies. And that became a -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very much part of the kind of legacy of Partisan culture in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in all of Yugoslavia. But in Prijedor in particular, the -- probably the most imposing monument to the Partisans and victims of World War II is located just outside Prijedor on -- at Mirkovica on Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In terms of its strategic position in the country in Bosnia-Herzegovina, why is Prijedor important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's located, first of all, in the heart of the Krajina. And it has a population that was mixed. It had no group with an absolute majority. Its Serbian population had been gradually declining, while its percentage of Muslims was gradually increasing. If I could just refer to page 49 of the report for a minute, one will see that it's about as close between the Muslims and Serbs as one can get. So the assembly -- municipal assembly elected in 1990 was also largely split between the HDZ -- SDA and SDS. It also has a relatively high percentage of Yugoslavs, reflecting that Partisan legacy and tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next document, which is Tab 26, Prosecutor's Exhibit 29. Briefly -- there is a English translation of this document. If you could summarise what the effect of the document is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the decision of the Serbian municipality of Kotor Varos on 7th February 1992 to join the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the next document which is behind Tab 27 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is an English translation for this document, which I've just discovered. I previously thought there was not a English translation. But I will wait to receive that in the courtroom before I actually refer to that document because it's quite important that the translation is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Dr. Donia, if you could go back to Tab 23, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 26. Now, this is a meeting, the twelfth session of the Serbian Assembly held on the 24th of March of 1992. And if you could go, please, to pages 23 and 24. And if you could explain to the Court the effect of that particular decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bottom of page 23 contains the decision of the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina to verify the establishment of new Serbian municipalities which would be in accord with those provisions of the directive of 19 December, 1991, and lists some, I think, 35 of them or so. So this is, in a sense, an inventory at this point in time of those SDS local boards that had complied with the directive and established a Serbian -- to the degree of establishing a Serbian Assembly of their municipality. There was further concern, however, expressed at this meeting that the task of forming Serbian assemblies in all municipalities had not been completed and not been completed properly. And on -- about one-third of the way down page 24, the chairperson, who would be Mr. Krajisnik, explained that, "All the presidents of autonomous districts had received instructions and should have prepared and organised this." This is a reference to the SAOs. "Those who have not done it should do so by Friday." I will represent to you that this was a Tuesday, so... "Can we verify this and finish what has not been done so far by Friday when we shall adopt the law? The assembly unanimously verifies the decisions by municipalities on the proclamation of newly established Serbian municipalities. Municipalities which have not done so shall submit by Friday their decisions verified by the competent organs." The date of Friday was simply the next scheduled session of the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this document speaks to the fact that the absence of a deadline in the document of 19 December had resulted in only partial compliance from the SDS local boards, and in those municipalities in which it was appropriate, it was to be completed now within three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can go back to tab 27, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 30, and I'll just hand out through the usher just the English version of this. I believe the B/C/S is complete. If it's not, we can correct that afterwards. Having checked the document, Mr. President, the B/C/S version, the version in Cyrillic, is complete. Do Your Honours have a copy of that document? Yes, I think the Defence do as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, if you go to the second page of the translation, which is the decision on the establishment of the Serbian Municipality of Donji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, I assume that this should now get a - maybe it already has - an evidence number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This would be 30A, P30A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "A"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So referring to Prosecutor's Exhibit 30A, Donji Vakuf, who was -- which ethnic group was in the majority in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a municipality with a majority of Muslim inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you go to the preamble to this decision, at the top of the page, on the -- it's the page that's numbered 1 at the bottom, but it's the second page of the translation, and you will see, Dr. Donia, on the fifth line, that, "This decision is being made pursuant to Article 4 of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances of 19 December, 1991." Dr. Donia, is that referring to the Variant A - Variant B document that we spoke about this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a reference to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And which variant was being implemented in this municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With less than 50 per cent Serbs, this would be a Variant B municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have anything else to say about this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the document is actually three related documents. The first page is a request for membership in the ARK and references two enclosures: number 1, the decision on establishing the Serbian municipality of Donji Vakuf on 15 February; and number 2, on the same session, or at the same date of 15 February, the decision of that municipality to join the ARK. This follows what I believe we saw earlier in Bihac, where the decision to join -- to create a Serbian municipality is followed, either immediately or after some brief period of time, with a decision to join the ARK. So this document speaks for the case of Donji Vakuf with the use of the Serbian assembly as a growth vehicle for the ARK. It recalls very similarly what was done by Mr. Vjestica in Bosanska Krupa and in, I think, Olovo, earlier. I would add that as I've surveyed the various reports in the periodical press, this was a not universal but common for those Serbia -- or those municipalities in which a Serbian municipality was organised, for a decision to join one of the SAOs to be taken simultaneously or shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on that note, if you go to tab 26, Prosecutor's Exhibit 29, this is a decision by the municipality of Kotor Varos. Does this reflect what you've just been saying to the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This would reflect the decision to join the ARK by Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can now move on to what is page 65 of your report. We're moving ahead in time now in respect of the whole of your report to January 1992. And this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 31, the 11th session of the assembly of the ARK. What was decided, Dr. Donia, at this particular meeting that's significant in terms of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this meeting of the ARK Assembly, the study of Bosnian Krajina as a constituent part of the new Yugoslav federation was given to each person. That's reflected on page 3 of this document, under section 3, the second sentence. And this study subsequently became the basis for several unanimously adopted recommendations. It will be recalled that the republic, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was declared on 9 January 1992. So this session is being held just one day before the Serbian Republic is proclaimed in Sarajevo. And of the recommendations is -- of note, number three, also under this section 3, on page 3 -- that "the assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it is constituted today, fulfil its function by defining and constituting Serbian regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which will be part of the Yugoslav state and through which they will be represented until the constitution of a future Yugoslav Assembly." So this request of the Serbian Assembly is to recognise the Serbian regions as a constituent part of the future Yugoslav Assembly, in a sense bypassing the actual Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and submitting them directly to be a part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On that note, if you go to the last page, page 4, of that document, where it begins, "It was decided at this session that a commission ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the significance of that paragraph in these minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this paragraph, the ARK Assembly is deciding to dispatch a commission directly to Belgrade to have talks with the Serbian president, Milosevic, as opposed to mediating that to the Assembly of the Serbian people or the Bosnian Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to two events: first of all, the declaration that the Bosnian Krajina is to be a part of the Yugoslav Federation; and secondly, the declaration of the Bosnian Serb Republic. Now, there was a third event that was taking place simultaneously at this time. And you've referred to it on page 65 of your report. And that was the recommendations of the Badinter Commission. Could you explain to the Court what those recommendations were and what the Badinter Commission actually was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I can return to this level of international negotiations for a moment. Once the international conference on Yugoslavia was established, it became evident in September 1991 that the solution to the war in Croatia was going to involve some form of recognition of a Serb -- or of a Croatian state and some element of a territorially distinct Serbian component within that state. At the same time, the republics of Slovenia and Croatia had declared independence back in June and agreed to defer the effectiveness of those declarations until October 8th, 1991. So with the background of these developments, the European Community sought to address the Yugoslav question consistently and on the basis of certain guidelines. It established the Badinter Commission to evaluate the applications of any Yugoslav republics that wished to apply for recognition of their independence. This was done in December 1991. And the Badinter Commission on 17 December 1991 invited applications from any Yugoslav republics wishing to apply for recognition. On the 20th of December, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted to apply for such independence. The decision was due -- the decision of the Badinter Commission was due on the 15th of January, 1992. While it was a foregone conclusion -- pretty much a foregone conclusion that this decision would award independence to Croatia and Slovenia, the situation on Bosnia-Herzegovina was less clear. And when the decision was announced on 15 January 1992, the Badinter Commission required that Bosnia-Herzegovina hold a referendum on independence if it wished to be recognised as an independent state by the European Community. Subsequently, both the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency voted to hold such a referendum on February 29 and March 1, 1992. In the shadow of these events, simultaneously with these events, of course, the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina made preparations in late December to proclaim a separate republic, and subsequently did so on 9 July -- or 9 January 1992. At the same time that the decision to form the republic was taken, it began preparations for a constitution of that republic and made plans to finalise or announce that constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the end of February 1992 roughly to coincide with the scheduled referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you brought us to the end of February. Let's go back to Banja Luka. And if I can take you to Tab 29, Prosecutor's Exhibit 32, which are minutes of the thirteenth session of the Assembly of the ARK. And the matters that you've broadly referred to are being discussed in these minutes. Can you draw the Judges' attentions to the relevant and pertinent parts of these minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ARK Assembly was discussing the provisions of the constitution of the Serbian republic to which I just referred. And on page 1 of this document, P32, at the very bottom, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin makes the statement that, "It is realistic to make Banja Luka the capital of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tomorrow in Sarajevo, we must all support the idea of cantons having the highest degree of autonomy." Now, this tomorrow in Sarajevo refers to a meeting to discuss the draft constitution of the Serbian Republic. And as a part of this meeting, there were decisions adopted on -- this is the third page of this document, the one -- the page has at the top of it Article 103(a). And at the very bottom of that page is the point 1, paragraph, "The following conclusions were adopted after a five-hour discussion. In order to preserve the unity of the Serbian people in BH and the SDS, the constituting of the Serbian Republic in BH is accepted but as a derived state structure to which the Serbian republics or cantons (as 'real states with genuine internal sovereignty') transfer some of their competence, or to be more precise, certain coordinating functions." So the ARK here is proposing that it interpose its authority and assert its sovereignty against the -- or within the Bosnian Serb Republic, much as the Bosnian Serb Republic had just -- was in the process of doing for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then turning the page, point 2, "Only Banja Luka, as the biggest city in BH in which the Serbs make up the absolute majority, can be the centre of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And finally, a threat, point 3, "If the Serbian Assembly of BH fails to accept the above-mentioned conclusions at its session on 25 and 26 February, that is, if BH is constituted as a unitary state with Sarajevo as its capital, as already intimated by the draft constitution," and then to the bottom of that paragraph, "On 28 February, the Krajina should be proclaimed a sovereign republic which will establish relations directly with other parts of BH." So this document then states the intent of the ARK, as adopted in these resolutions, to declare itself a sovereign republic if the Serbian Republic does not recognise it and give it substantial autonomy in its constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if you can now go to the next binder, and indeed if we could all do that now, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your evidence that the ARK assembly had referred to a meeting that was to take place the next day, and the next day after the 24th of February was the 25th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm right in saying that that meeting was the eighth session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Prosecutor's Exhibit 33 Alpha are the minutes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to orientate us in respect of events going on generally at the international level, what had Dr. Karadzic been up to during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the early months of 1992, talks were convened by the Conference on Yugoslavia in Lisbon - not Brussels, Lisbon - and on the 17th of February, 1992, an agreement in principle was reached by the three principals from Bosnia, that is Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Mr. Mate Boban, I believe, and the -- Mr. Izetbegovic. This was essentially an agreement to partition Bosnia into three distinct parts. And upon returning to Sarajevo after the conclusion of this agreement in principle, which was to be followed by further negotiations, Dr. Karadzic addressed the eighth session of the assembly and was quite ecstatic, in fact, about the achievement of having a separate Serbian entity recognised through these negotiations, and the early pages of this document reflect that enthusiasm for the negotiations as they had proceeded that far. But suddenly, on page 11 of this document, towards the bottom of the page, we see that Mr. Karadzic's remarks were interrupted by a telephone call from Mr. Jose Cutilliero, and he left the assembly hall with apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was Jose Cutilliero?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Cutilliero was in charge of -- he was the coordinator, the convenor, of those negotiations in Lisbon on behalf of the Conference on the Yugoslavia. When he left the hall, as can be seen, Professor Nikola Koljevic proceeded to do what I think is called, in the radio business, filling air, and talked for several pages about the negotiations and similarly shared Dr. Karadzic's enthusiasm. On page 13, about one-quarter of the way down the page, we see that Dr. Karadzic returns to the assembly hall and Professor Koljevic continues his speech on to page 14, and in that last paragraph on page 14, I think he puts the achievement in pretty good perspective, actually. Where he says, in the last paragraph, "Another general impression, I believe that after the establishment of the SDS and then regionalisation, this is the third political event in order of importance." And he's referring here to this agreement in principle reached in Lisbon. "It is a step in the direction of winning back the disenfranchised rights that the Serbian people were deprived of in these parts." So he gives the -- attributes great importance to this achievement of a separate Serbian state, agreed in principle at Lisbon. When Dr. Karadzic resumes, however, he reports on his conversation with Cutilliero and states that Cutilliero has received a letter from Izetbegovic and that letter, which was published all over the world at that time, basically stated that due to events in Banja Luka and the convening of an assembly in Banja Luka in which it was discussed that there will be a constitution proclaimed for the Bosnian Serb Republic, he found further discussions on this agreement to be pointless. So in the immediate aftermath of this discussion of Cutilliero's interrupting phone call, Karadzic became very -- expressed extreme displeasure with the autonomous direction that was being taken by the ARK assembly. If one goes to page 17, the third line - and recalling that it was their intention to accept the draft constitution that day - Karadzic says, "It would not be a good idea to adopt the constitution today as that would be a reason for Cutilliero not to come." They were planning to reconvene these discussions in Sarajevo. "Or to make any move which might affect what we agree today. He told me today, 'Fine, if you can keep the Serbs quiet,' and I explained that this thing in Krajina reflected their distrust of Alija Izetbegovic with whom we had talked for three months at a time. And just as we thought we had reached an agreement, he would come up with a completely different document, which is why the Serbs do not trust him." But it subsequently became evident that Karadzic's irritation with -- or blaming this on Izetbegovic did not just stop him from also blaming those in the Krajina who were pursuing an autonomous course and resisting the authority of the SDS main board. On page 44, the second full paragraph: "Of course the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will have its regents with full freedom to act according to the interests of the Serbian people. However, I promise you, Bosnian Krajina must not become an issue. If it becomes an issue, then we will lose the Knin Krajina." The Krajina across the border in Croatia. "Alija is praying to God that we succeed, that we screw up. They will send in UN forces, create zone A and zone B, and we are certain to lose one of them, and the other will be part of an independent BH with all sorts of conditions imposed." And then one paragraph down: "We cannot allow that five people with personal ambitions destroy our chances. We are very close to achieving our strategic objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who is speaking there, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic is speaking. That's identified on page 42. Now, on page 74, we see the resolution that was proposed by assembly president Krajisnik at this time, which was to convene a session of the ARK Assembly in Banja Luka and have it attended by essentially the entire senior leadership of the SDS party in order to persuade them to accept the constitution -- the draft constitution of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any further comments on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now go to Tab 30, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 34. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, this is a transcript of the meeting of the deputy's club of the Serbian Democratic party held in Sarajevo on the 28th of February, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you draw the Court's attention to the significant parts of this document. And just -- just to clarify matters, this particular meeting takes place three days after the assembly meeting that you've just been referring to, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is on 28 February, and it was held at -- in the morning. On the second page, we see it began at 10.30 hours. And in the afternoon, there was another session of the Serbian Assembly. So this meeting preceded that meeting, and the afternoon meeting resulted in the adoption of a constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But it was at this earlier meeting of the SDS deputies that the issue of the ARK was again addressed and some -- many complaints were launched about the, let's say, wilfulness or assertions of the ARK leadership. On page 28, the speaker, Mr. Marinko Kontic -- about two-thirds of the way down the page, the paragraph begins: "The problem in Banja Luka. And I will tell you who the people need to be marked are: the President of the Assembly, Radic, and Mr. Brdjanin, whom I have feared from day one. I have had a few clashes with him, and I think there's something wrong with him. There is a sickness in that man who always wants to be the boss, and he's interested only in power. There is some other people there too." I would note that Kontic goes on to defend Vojo Kupresanin, the president of the ARK Assembly. The next speaker here is -- or a couple of speakers later is Dr. Karadzic, who begins speaking on 33, and on page 36 makes further references to the Krajina. About three-quarters of the way down the paragraph, it begins: "We can and we must renounce everyone who refuses to work the way we have agreed, Brdjo and all the rest. When Brdjo appears somewhere, he's like a bomb. He blows everything up. Then he winks at him. And I won't allow it as a psychiatrist and as the party leader." The solution that emerged from this particular session was essentially to blame the difficulties, the kind of self-will of the Krajina Assembly, on five or six individuals who were kind of second-tier members of the assembly, and then to adopt within the actual constitution of the Serbian republic a recognition of the existence of the Serbian autonomous regions but without specifying that the -- the concession was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that they didn't specify that the territory of the Serbian republic was indivisible. They did, however, identify or define the territory of the Serbian republic as made up of the territories of the Serbian autonomous regions, and in a number of constitutional provisions, starting with Article 100 to about 108, assigned them certain functions constitutionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next day, the 29th of February of 1992, and we'll go back to Banja Luka. And if I can direct you to Tab 31, Prosecutor's Exhibit 35, which is an extract from the minutes of the fourteenth session of the Assembly of the ARK. First of all, who attended this meeting? Specifically, I'm referring to people from, as it were, the republican level SDS party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attendees given in the third paragraph here comprised most of the senior leaders of the SDS. Consequently, this is the realisation of Mr. Krajisnik's proposal that all of the senior members of the SDS descend on Banja Luka and attend this session. So Radovan Karadzic is present, Krajisnik, Nikola Koljevic, and Velibor Ostojic, who is the Minister of Information. In number one of this extract, the second paragraph, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, the Vice-President of the Assembly of the autonomous region, I think in a wonderful understatement, recalled that the deputies in this assembly, that is the ARK, "had reached an agreement at the previous session on the integrity of the republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina but with a different viewpoint compared to the one offered to the people of the Krajina from the centre in Sarajevo." On the next page, we see at the top that Dr. Karadzic spoke and then that the ARK Assembly voted to accept his report on the political and security situation in full, that under the section labelled "Conclusion." And this compromise, which brings the ARK under the umbrella of the Serbian Republic, is expressed in the next two paragraphs there. "Jovan Cizmovic, coordinator in the Serbian government BH, recalled that the ARK can draw its autonomy from the recently adopted constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that if a republic of Krajina were declared, all Serbs outside this territory would suffer from the consequences of this decision." So they backed down from the idea of an independent or sovereign republic. And in the second paragraph there, Radovan Karadzic stressed that "it would be a crime against the Krajina if it were declared a republic." On the next page, point one, the deputies in the Assembly of the ARK accepted the constitution of the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina in full. This meeting essentially brought to an end the clash between the ARK and the central leadership of the SDS regarding its status under that constitutional document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if we can now go to Tab 33, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 37. And this -- and this is the instruction regarding the conduct of the plebiscite of the Muslim and Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is an instruction from the Serbian Assembly of the ARK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's from the ARK Assembly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And just to clarify matters, this is the -- referring to the plebiscite or referendum that you previously spoke of that had been recommended by the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
